1:
That the distance is apparent rather than real is agreed, and each accounts for it differently. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) turns the complaint back on the complainer: outward deliverance is hidden from us and we therefore think God afar off, but that is our own fault, for we judge by outward appearance, and we stand afar off from God by our unbelief and then complain that he stands afar off from us. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) answers it with an image instead, that the refiner is never far from the mouth of the furnace when his gold is in the fire, and adds that it is not the trouble but the hiding of our Father’s face which cuts us to the quick. Augustine of Hippo (latin-fathers) makes the delay deliberate: God despises seasonably, and causes tribulations to inflame men’s minds with longing for his coming, since that fountain of life is sweeter to them that have much thirst.

What kind of psalm this is divides the critics from the preachers. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note it is one of only two anonymous psalms in the first book, and defend the Septuagint’s joining of it to the preceding psalm as not without warrant, on the ground of the acrostic, this psalm beginning in the middle of the alphabet with the letter that continues the preceding psalm’s order. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reaches the same joining from the manuscripts, that the psalm forms part of the preceding in the Vulgate and Septuagint and in several of the collated codices; but he departs from the others on the occasion, taking it to belong to the time of the captivity or the return, and probably composed with reference to Sanballat and the other enemies of the Jews. John Calvin (reformed) keeps it David’s own, complaining in his name and in the name of all the godly that fraud and extortion and cruelty prevailed everywhere, and reads the whole as a mirror of a corrupt society, into which the faithful should look when iniquity breaks out like a flood, since it lightens grief that nothing befalls us which the Church has not known of old.

Who it is that burns, and who is taken in the devices, is a genuine quarrel over the Hebrew. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) would render it that in the pride of the wicked the sufferer burns, following the Septuagint and the Vulgate, and insists the word is not of indignation but literally of the afflictions they endure; in the next clause he takes the humble rather than the wicked as the subject, since that preserves the parallelism, so that the sufferers are taken in the plot the wicked devised. John Gill (reformed) reads the verb with the Jewish commentators as following after and pursuing hotly, which denotes the vehemence and heat of the persecutor’s fury. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the boasting instead, that far from hiding the shameful desire of his soul the wicked man makes it a ground of high and sounding praise, imagining himself above all restraint human or divine; and they reject Hupfeld’s rendering of the clause outright.

Spurgeon alone reads the verse as a legal proceeding, finding in it the formal indictment against the wicked, which divides into the two charges of pride and tyranny, the one the root and cause of the other, followed by the humble petition of the oppressed; and he defends its justice on the ground that men should be done by as they wished to do to others, since we only weigh them in their own scales. Gill alone looks past the immediate oppressor to a figure, making the wicked one the lawless one, the man of sin and son of perdition, the great persecutor of Christ’s poor saints and faithful witnesses.
3:
One phrase about the wicked man’s ways is rendered five ways. John Gill (reformed) surveys four of them, that his ways cause terror and make men fear, or are defiled as the Greek and Latin have it, or always remain the same with no change in them for the better, or else prosper, which he notes is sometimes stumbling to the saints. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) prefers that his enterprises always succeed, taking the sense from a cognate meaning strength and from a parallel in Job, though he allows that always strong may imply only the bold and reckless course with which a tyrant pursues his end. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads something quite different, that the man is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity at all times, conceiving and bringing forth sin until death is brought forth with it. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) secure the sense of lasting or stiff from the same passage in Job: he takes whatever ways he chooses and they always lead to the desired end, so that he neither stumbles nor goes astray.

Ellicott spends much of this portrait correcting the received translation. On the boast he gives the literal sense as speaking praise to the lust of his own soul, and finds the representation of a villain addressing his evil passions in laudatory terms highly poetic, comparing the rich fool of the parable congratulating his soul upon his greed; where the English has blessing the covetous he reads cursing instead, by a common euphemism. On the next verse he says roundly that the Authorised Version has quite missed the meaning, and would render that the wicked in his haughtiness — literally the height of his nostril — says that God will not requite it, and that there is no God in all his thought. Clarke redivides the same clause to different effect, so that it is the wicked man who abhors the Lord rather than the Lord who abhors the covetous: those like himself he commends and associates with, and they have a mortal hatred of everything holy.

Where the ambushes are laid decides what sort of man this is, and here they part. Gill observes that the word signifies palaces or courts, as the Chaldee and Syriac render it, so that the allusion is not to mean thieves and robbers at all but to persons of note and figure, the Greek and Latin and Arabic versions giving that he sits in lurking places with the rich. Ellicott takes the word properly of enclosed spaces, and then of any collection of dwellings, noting that elsewhere it is used of an unwalled place and even of a nomadic encampment. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keeps the highwayman, placing him not within the villages but in the ways bordering upon them or leading to them, as robbers use to do. Clarke finds here an allusion to espionage, the setting of spies on a man’s conduct, or the conduct of an assassin.

The lion and the net are noticed as an awkwardness. Ellicott calls it plainly a confusion of metaphor, the wicked being first the lion watching for his prey and then the hunter snaring animals, and he renders it as lurking in his lair to seize a sufferer, and seizing him, drawing him into the net. Keil and Delitzsch see the figure of the lion reversed in the second line. Clarke keeps the two together without complaint, likening him to a hunter who lays traps and gins, digs pits and sets nets, and destroys the prey when it falls in. Through the whole portrait Gill alone reads an allegory, finding here the mouth of the first beast and the speech of the second, the insidious methods of a power that has two horns like a lamb and yet calls itself the servant of servants.
12:
The prayer is admired, and its inconsistency noticed. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) marks both at once: with what bold language will faith address its God, and yet what unbelief is mingled with our strongest confidence, since the Lord is fearlessly stirred up to arise and lift up his hand and then timidly begged not to forget the humble, as if he could ever be forgetful of his saints.. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) asks for something more final, that God would arise to the confusion of those who say he hides his face and lift up his hand to give a fatal blow to the oppressors. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads the same clause as a threat rather than a stroke, that he would lift up his hand to warn them so they may desist and repent, and only if they repent not let them be punished. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes in passing that the acrostic arrangement is resumed at this verse.

Why such men are suffered to go on draws three different answers. Clarke turns the delay into mercy: how does the Lord permit them to triumph in their iniquity? Because his longsuffering leads them to repentance. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) puts it far more sharply: why dost thou, by giving them impunity, suffer and occasion them to despise thee? Spurgeon traces the evil to its source instead, in atheistical ideas about the government of the world, and makes the whole passage an urgent plea for God to show his power — when the wicked call his righteousness in question, we may well beg him to teach them terrible things in righteousness. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) answer the wicked man’s premise directly: he thinks God will not punish, but God does see, and the psalmist knows and confesses it.

On the committing of the helpless to God, Ellicott alone will not leave the text as it stands. He would render that the helpless leaves it to Thee, and then observes that a slight alteration in the division of the Hebrew letters and the pointing would give something quite different, that it is against Thee that he is strong in darkness — turning the clause from the sufferer’s trust into the oppressor’s defiance. The others read it devotionally and without hesitation. Clarke has the poor man giving up to God his body, his soul and his cause, in the full conviction that the helper of the fatherless will not forget him. John Gill (reformed) fastens on the preceding clause, that though the wicked say God will never see, he sees all men and all their actions, even what is thought in the heart.

The last petition produces a flat philological collision, and the two sides appeal to the same evidence. Ellicott holds the sense clear from two passages elsewhere, where to seek and not find is a proverb expressing the riddance of evil, though he grants the construction is difficult and would end the first clause early, rendering that as for the evil man, thou shalt look for his wickedness and not find it. Keil and Delitzsch cite those very same two passages to the opposite purpose: it is a mistake, they say, to treat the two verbs here as correlative notions, because in the phrase to seek and not find, used of what has totally disappeared, the Hebrew never employs the verb that stands in this verse but always a different one — which is precisely the verb those parallels use. Clarke offers two renderings without choosing, that the man’s haunts shall all be investigated and punishment continue while there is a crime to punish, or that God will judge transgressors till not one is found. Wesley takes it of searching out wickedness until none be left in the world, or at least in the church.
16:
The close is felt as a change of key. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) puts it briefly, that if the psalm has hitherto been personal it here swells out into a larger strain of national hope and faith. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) describe the poet as standing on an eminence from which he seems to behold the end, basking in what has been obtained in answer to prayer, the longing of the meek and lowly for the Lord’s arising having now been heard. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) reads it as thanksgiving and draws the lesson, that we are sure to speed well if we carry our complaint to the King of kings, since rights will be vindicated at his throne, and his government neither neglects the needy nor tolerates oppression in the mighty. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) grounds the comfort in the office itself, that it belongs to a king to protect his subjects, so that his people’s case is never desperate while he ever lives to help them.

Which heathen have perished, and out of whose land, is answered historically by two and prophetically by a third. Wesley takes them for the Canaanites, whom God as king of the world expelled to give their land to his people, and reads the land as his because he gave it to them and fixed his dwelling in it, a great example by which faith is confirmed for the future. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) agrees it may refer to the Canaanites, adding that they were either cut off or converted, and then turns it upon his own country with evident feeling: once it was entirely heathen, and now there is not one heathen family in the whole land. John Gill (reformed) looks the other way, forward rather than back, taking the King to be Christ, who reigned from everlasting and was promised as King under the old dispensation, appeared more visibly in that office at his ascension, and will be yet more manifestly King of saints in the latter day.

On the preparing of the heart, two voices from opposite sides of the old division say the same thing. Clarke sets out an economy of grace in four steps, that God prepares the heart, suggests the prayer, hears what is prayed and answers the petition; from which he concludes that a man with a cry in his heart after God may rest assured it proceeded from a divine preparation, and that he who continues to cry shall infallibly be heard. Gill reaches the same point from his own side, observing that the prayers of God’s people sometimes lie in inward and secret desires never expressed in words, that these desires are all before the Lord and principally regarded by him, and that they are his own preparation.

The last line is retranslated twice, and differently. Clarke believes the Hebrew better rendered that the oppressor may not add any more to drive away the wretched man from the land, so that the prayer is for the tyrant’s influence to be destroyed and for him never again to have power to add even one further act of oppression; and he applies it to those who, for their religion’s sake, have been driven off their farms and turned out of their houses by wicked lords and arrogant landowners. Ellicott takes the words quite otherwise, rendering literally that he may not continue to terrify, or to defy, mere man from the earth, which he thinks may mean that mere mortals shall have to confess their weakness; and on the oppressed of the same verse he borrows a sentence from Leighton, that God’s choice acquaintances are humble men. Gill keeps to his own reading throughout, that God will avenge the wrongs done to the fatherless and to those oppressed by the man of sin.
